rule: Read the current state of a record with a typed read ability before mutating it.
why: Blind writes overwrite settings the caller never saw and cannot roll back accurately.

rule: Snapshot the target before mutating an Elementor document, a template, a global-styles record, or theme.json-backed content.
why: A snapshot is the only reliable rollback boundary for builder payloads.

rule: Re-read the mutated record after every write and confirm the intended values are present before reporting success.
why: Builder and cache layers can silently drop or coerce values.

rule: Validate a design spec with the design-spec validator before handing it to any renderer.
why: Invalid specs produce broken markup that then needs a destructive repair.

rule: Never JSON-encode an already-encoded Elementor data payload.
why: Double encoding makes the document unreadable to the editor and unrecoverable without a snapshot.

rule: Never drop settings the local schema does not recognise in order to pass validation.
why: Unknown keys usually belong to a newer builder version or a third-party widget and are load-bearing.

rule: Never change an element widget type to make a control writable. Ask for explicit intent first.
why: Type conversion silently discards every setting the old type owned.

rule: Fix one control with a targeted batch mutation on that element. Never rewrite the whole element tree.
why: Full-tree rewrites reintroduce every defect the tree already had and lose unmodelled state.

rule: Target a breakpoint on a style control with the builder breakpoint suffix on the base control key; do not invent per-breakpoint control names.
why: Only suffixed variants of responsive base controls are read by the builder.

rule: Treat visibility controls whose names end in a breakpoint word as standalone booleans, not breakpoint variants of a style control.
why: They exist at every breakpoint scope and are rejected wrongly when parsed as suffixed style keys.

rule: Read the live schema for a widget, block, field group, or post type before writing to it. Consult official documentation when the schema is unknown.
why: Guessed control keys write dead data that looks like a successful mutation.

rule: Use the typed tool surface. Do not hand-roll protocol calls, scratch runner scripts, helper argument files, shell CLI invocations, or direct ability-run endpoints to work around a missing tool.
why: Workarounds bypass permission, backup, validation, confirmation, and audit gates.

rule: If a required tool is absent from the client tool list, run the surface check and reactivate the profile, then ask the user to reload the client. Do not substitute another transport.
why: A missing tool is a configuration fault, not a reason to leave the sanctioned path.

rule: Send code with real newlines and real indentation. Never send a multi-statement file as one line with escape sequences.
why: Escaped one-liners land in editors unreadable and defeat diff review.

rule: A complete PHP file candidate must pass in-process syntax validation before it is written.
why: An unparseable theme file takes the whole site down.

rule: In production-safe mode obtain and pass a confirmation token for every destructive operation.
why: It is the only interlock between an agent and irreversible production damage.

rule: Capture fresh evidence for the current revision before reporting a visual result. Evidence from a previous revision does not count.
why: Stale evidence is how a broken layout gets reported as done.

rule: Group related element mutations into one batch call instead of issuing one call per control.
why: Each round trip re-sends context and multiplies the chance of a partially applied change.

rule: When a feature flag disables a renderer or ability, report the flag and stop. Do not route around it.
why: The flag encodes an operator decision about experimental surface.

rule: When the user corrects a repeatable mistake, record it as a learning entry in the same session.
why: Uncaptured corrections recur and cost the user the same explanation twice.

rule: Never remove a permission, backup, validation, confirmation, audit, test, or source-verification step to reduce token cost or latency.
why: Every one of those steps exists because its absence already caused damage once.
